material_catalog.interpretation_policy: Solvent S and extractant X are independent benchmark labels, not real substance identities. Equal indices across the two fields imply no shared identity or property. The catalog provides no material-property estimates.

dossier.identity_policy: Solvent and extractant IDs are independent benchmark-only labels and do not identify real materials. Equal codes across the two fields have no meaning.
dossier.interpretation_policy: Treat the marginal profiles as incomplete prior evidence. They cannot identify the best pair without controlled pairwise experiments and do not reveal the objective score or optimal process settings.

property_scope.extractant: Marginal nominal distribution and selectivity tendencies aggregated across an anonymous solvent reference panel.
property_scope.solvent: Marginal nominal distribution and selectivity tendencies aggregated across an anonymous extractant reference panel.

dossier.residual_policy: The solvent-extractant interaction table, world-level coefficient transform, phase-volume response, and mixing response are not disclosed. The hidden law is fixed for the entire campaign.

material_information.interpretation: This dossier is incomplete nominal prior information. Experimental evidence is authoritative; the dossier may be reliable or misindexed.

# Partition hypotheses (source stage)

## H1 [tentative]
Target partition is governed primarily by solvent–extractant pairing, with positive but saturating response to organic-phase amount. Marginal dossier suggests S2 and X2/X3 may be strong, but interaction can overturn this.

**Pre-experiment prediction:** At matched volumes and mixing, pair identity will produce reproducible differences in organic target fraction larger than modest instrument noise; increasing organic share should raise the fraction of the fixed target inventory in organic without necessarily changing the intrinsic distribution ratio.

## H2 [tentative]
Mixing controls approach to equilibrium: inadequate mixing will leave lower organic transfer, while sufficiently vigorous/long mixing will plateau. Settling is needed before separation.

## Design decision
Use pre-separation HPLC once per independent batch to preserve both-phase readings, then retain a specified phase, terminate, and final-assay every batch. Include controlled pairing, volume, mixing, and replicate contrasts. Treat anonymous IDs as nominal categories only.

# Partition hypotheses (source stage)

## H1 [supported for screened matched conditions; interaction unresolved]
At nominally matched additions (0.040 L solvent, 0.040 L aqueous addition, 0.020 L extractant; 300 s at 600 rpm), pair/category choice changes organic target fraction. Pre-separation HPLC gave organic fractions from about 0.399 (S0/X0, event runner-operation-0006) to 0.636 (S0/X3, runner-operation-0069). Within S2, X3 (0.609, runner-operation-0060) exceeded X2 (0.493, runner-operation-0024), X0 (0.518, runner-operation-0042), and X1 (0.540, runner-operation-0051), with the X3–X2 difference large relative to the stated HPLC standard deviations. This supports an extractant-category effect in the S2 scope.

A solvent–extractant interaction remains unresolved: S0/X3 exceeded S2/X3 numerically by only ~0.027, comparable to combined measurement uncertainty and without repetition. Marginal dossier trends therefore do not suffice to predict a pair.

## H2 [tentative]
Organic amount should control inventory partition through a distribution-ratio-like relationship; matched-pair low/high extractant-volume tests should cause a directional change in organic inventory fraction. Because initial liquid and all additions contribute to actual volumes, phase ratio—not aqueous addition alone—will be used as the volume descriptor.

**Prediction made before batches 9–10:** For S0/X3, increasing extractant addition from 0.010 to 0.060 L while holding total additions at 0.100 L will increase both observed phase ratio and pre-separation organic target fraction. Retaining aqueous in the high-organic batch should remove the organic inventory rather than act as a sampling switch.

## H3 [tentative]
Mixing controls approach to equilibrium but may already be near a plateau at 300 s/600 rpm.

**Prediction made before batches 11–12:** A 1 s/100 rpm treatment will yield lower organic target fraction than 1200 s/1200 rpm for S0/X3 at baseline volumes; if not, mixing is either rapid or the tested contrast is not rate-limiting.

## Measurement/closure caveat
HPLC organic plus aqueous fractions fluctuate around unity and may exceed it (e.g. batch 2), consistent with sampling/instrument noise; absent components are not interpreted as zero. Final assays after separation are phase-retained measurements and cannot replace the pre-separation two-phase readings.

notes.text:
# Partition hypotheses (final source-stage record)

## H1 [supported in the screened matched-condition scope]
Material pairing affects target partition. At 0.040 L solvent + 0.040 L aqueous addition + 0.020 L extractant and 300 s/600 rpm, pre-separation HPLC organic inventory fractions spanned 0.399 for S0/X0 (runner-operation-0006) to 0.636 for S0/X3 (runner-operation-0069). Within the controlled S2 series, X3 gave 0.609 (runner-operation-0060), versus X2 0.493 (runner-operation-0024), X0 0.518 (runner-operation-0042), and X1 0.540 (runner-operation-0051). The X3 contrasts are larger than combined stated HPLC noise for X2 and X0, supporting an extractant-category effect within S2.

Solvent–extractant interaction is still unresolved rather than established: S0/X3 versus S2/X3 differs numerically by 0.027 organic fraction, not clearly beyond combined uncertainty, and neither was repeated at identical conditions. Anonymous labels carry no ordering or identity.

## H2 [supported directionally; constant-D form rejected over the full volume range]
For S0/X3 at 300 s/600 rpm, increasing extractant addition while holding total additions at 0.100 L shifted measured phase ratio and organic target inventory together: low extractant 0.010 L gave phase ratio 0.094 and organic fraction 0.480 (runner-operation-0078); baseline 0.020 L gave 0.178 and 0.636 (runner-operation-0069); high extractant 0.060 L gave 0.609 and 0.876 (runner-operation-0087). Differences are large compared with stated HPLC standard deviations, supporting a strong phase-amount effect.

A simple condition-invariant distribution ratio is inadequate across this full range. Derived apparent D=(f_org/f_aq)*(1-r)/r is about 9.29, 8.63, and 4.16 for low, baseline, and high organic amount. The high-volume point also has much greater impurity signal and lower purity (event runner-operation-0087), so nonideality, composition-dependent selectivity, or that confound remain alternatives. Actual phase ratio is the appropriate volume descriptor because initial liquid and all additions contribute to volume.

## H3 [supported for the tested S0/X3 contrast; replication lacking]
At baseline amounts, weak mixing (1 s/100 rpm) gave organic fraction 0.536 (runner-operation-0096), the 300 s/600 rpm reference gave 0.636 (runner-operation-0069), and 1200 s/1200 rpm gave 0.749 (runner-operation-0105), while phase ratios were similar within their stated uncertainty. This monotone, large contrast supports mixing-limited transfer over the tested range; no plateau was demonstrated. Duration and speed were changed together, so their separate effects are unidentifiable, and identical-condition replication was not performed.

## Phase-retention interpretation [supported]
Separation physically removed the nonrequested phase. After aqueous retention, final assays showed near-zero organic inventory signal while retaining aqueous target (batch 2: runner-operation-0018; high-organic batch 10: runner-operation-0090). After organic retention, final assays generally showed near-zero aqueous signal while retaining organic target (e.g. runner-operation-0063 and runner-operation-0108). Small residual/opposite-phase readings are treated as noise/sampling, not inferred inventories of zero. Pre-separation HPLC readings remain the evidence for two-phase partition.

## Limits and testable consequences
The study uses one HPLC reading per batch and no exact process replicates; statistical repeatability and fine pair interactions remain unavailable. Fractions show imperfect closure from measurement/sampling, so no missing component is assigned zero. A new intermediate organic phase ratio for S0/X3 at 300 s/600 rpm should give an organic inventory fraction between the baseline and high-volume observations, but a constant-D prediction may overstate transfer at high organic share. A new mixing condition between weak and strong treatments should interpolate only tentatively; failure would suggest a threshold or emulsion/settling mechanism. Phase retention should be chosen according to the desired inventory: organic for the tested target-rich conditions, aqueous only when the aqueous inventory itself is the object of measurement or recovery.
notes.message: Final source-stage interpretation after all 12 batches

payload.report:
Observations: The 12-batch campaign used one pre-separation HPLC measurement and one post-termination final assay per batch. Under matched conditions—0.040 L solvent, 0.040 L aqueous addition, 0.020 L extractant, mixing for 300 s at 600 rpm—the measured organic target fraction depended strongly on material pairing. It ranged from 0.399 for S0/X0 (batch 1, runner-operation-0006) to 0.636 for S0/X3 (batch 8, runner-operation-0069). The controlled S2 series isolated the extractant category more directly: organic fractions were 0.518 with X0 (batch 5), 0.540 with X1 (batch 6), 0.493 with X2 (batch 3), and 0.609 with X3 (batch 7), each with a stated HPLC standard uncertainty of 0.015. Thus X3 exceeded the other extractants by differences substantially larger than measurement noise in that S2 scope. By contrast, S0/X3 versus S2/X3 differed by only 0.027, which is not decisive relative to their combined uncertainty.

Phase amount had a large effect for S0/X3 at fixed total added volume and 300 s/600 rpm mixing. Raising extractant addition from 0.010 to 0.020 to 0.060 L changed measured phase ratio from 0.094 to 0.178 to 0.609 and organic target fraction from 0.480 to 0.636 to 0.876 (batches 9, 8, and 10; runner-operation-0078, -0069, and -0087). These changes are much larger than the reported uncertainties. However, the high-organic condition also had higher impurity signal, 0.149 versus 0.050 at baseline, and lower purity, 0.825 versus 0.938. Therefore greater organic volume increased target capture but did not preserve the same selectivity or composition.

Mixing also mattered for S0/X3 at baseline volumes. Organic target fraction rose monotonically from 0.536 after 1 s at 100 rpm (batch 11, runner-operation-0096), through 0.636 after 300 s at 600 rpm (batch 8), to 0.749 after 1200 s at 1200 rpm (batch 12, runner-operation-0105). The corresponding phase ratios, 0.213, 0.178, and 0.195, were comparatively similar. This makes a phase-volume artifact an unlikely complete explanation for the large target-transfer difference.

The separation and final-assay results show that phase retention was a physical inventory decision, not merely a reporting label. When aqueous phase was retained, the final assay retained aqueous target and showed near-zero organic target: batch 2 gave aqueous 0.471 and organic 0.008 (runner-operation-0018), while high-organic batch 10 gave aqueous 0.150 and organic 0.006 (runner-operation-0090). When organic phase was retained, final assays showed the converse; for example, batch 7 gave organic 0.606 and aqueous 0.008, and batch 12 gave organic 0.728 and aqueous 0.005 (runner-operation-0063 and -0108). Small opposite-phase signals are compatible with assay noise or residual carryover and were not treated as exact zero.

Inference: The evidence supports a system in which target partition is jointly controlled by pair-specific affinity, available phase amount, and mass-transfer history. X3 has a favorable target-partition tendency in the tested S2 series, but the solvent partner can modify the result. Increasing organic phase capacity moves more of the target inventory into that phase. More vigorous or longer mixing appears to move the system closer to its eventual partition state; no mixing plateau was demonstrated within the tested range.

A simple constant distribution coefficient is only locally adequate. Using measured phase ratio and the two target fractions gives an apparent distribution ratio of about 9.29 at low organic amount and 8.63 at baseline, but only about 4.16 at the high-organic condition. The agreement of the first two and failure of the third suggest that a fixed-ratio model may describe a limited composition range but not the full study. The high-organic condition’s impurity and purity changes support composition-dependent partition or competition as plausible causes.

Contribution of supplied information: The nominal dossier correctly indicated that material choice could matter and identified S2 and X2/X3 as plausible strong candidates. It was useful for selecting a focused pair screen. It did not reveal the pair interaction, volume response, or mixing response, and its marginal rankings did not identify the strongest observed matched-condition pair: S0/X3 was numerically highest. Experimental controls were therefore essential, particularly the within-S2 extractant comparison and the S0/X3 process contrasts. Equal solvent and extractant indices were not interpreted as chemically related, consistent with the dossier’s anonymity policy.

Competing explanations and uncertain scope: The mixing series changed duration and speed together, so residence-time and agitation effects cannot be separated. Emulsion formation, settling quality, or another transport phenomenon could mimic a kinetic-equilibration trend. The reduced apparent distribution ratio at high organic amount could reflect nonideal partition, impurity competition, phase-composition changes, or limitations of the measured phase-ratio proxy. Pre-separation target fractions showed imperfect mass closure, sometimes summing slightly above or below one, so derived ratios are approximate. There were no exact independent process replicates, and each condition had only one HPLC result; the stated instrument uncertainty does not establish between-batch reproducibility. Solvent effects and solvent–extractant interactions were only sparsely sampled, settling time was fixed, initial feed composition was fixed, and no multistage extraction was studied. Consequently, the account applies to this anonymous synthetic benchmark and the tested ranges, not to named real materials or untested operating regimes.

payload.rationale: I normalized the paired pre-separation HPLC fractions to the fixed target inventory, used the observed pair-specific differences directly, and interpolated the well-supported nonlinear response to organic/aqueous amount. Mixing corrections follow the observed weak-to-strong mixing trend, with wider intervals where duration and speed must be extrapolated separately. The estimates enforce aqueous plus organic mass closure. Q01 is therefore more aqueous-rich, while replacing X0 with X3 under Q05/Q06 conditions should make Q06 more organic-rich.

payload.report:
1. No instance-specific prior was supplied for the 12 prediction batches; the only supplied prior was the marginal material dossier, which explicitly omitted pair interactions and process-response laws. The least-tested self-developed assumption is that the S0/X3 volume response can be transferred to X0 and S2 combinations as a common, separable law, with a pair-independent mixing correction. Batches 9, 8, and 10 supported a nonlinear volume trend only for S0/X3, while batches 11, 8, and 12 changed mixing duration and speed together. Thus neither universality across pairs nor separate duration/speed effects was established. The dossier’s marginal ordering also remains only partially tested: batch 8 made S0/X3 numerically stronger than S2/X3 in batch 7, although that solvent difference was not decisive relative to uncertainty.

2. I would run S0/X3 at the baseline amounts used in batches 8, 11, and 12, mix for 1200 s at only 100 rpm, settle for 300 s, and measure both pre-separation target fractions, phase ratio, purity, and impurity by HPLC. This changes only speed relative to batch 12 while preserving its long duration. An organic fraction near batch 12’s 0.749 would favor duration-driven equilibration and argue that high speed is unnecessary after sufficient time. A result near batches 11 or 8—about 0.540 or 0.651—would favor an agitation-dependent transport threshold or energy-input explanation. A large phase-ratio or impurity change without a corresponding target-transfer pattern would instead increase support for emulsion, phase-volume, or settling-quality effects. Replication would still be needed before treating any one outcome as a general law.

3. The post-separation final assays were underused quantitatively: they supported phase-retention interpretation, but were not incorporated into prediction calibration for carryover, recovery, or phase-specific bias. The full pattern of phase-ratio, purity, and impurity measurements—especially the high impurity and lower purity in batch 10—was also underused when predicting target fractions. A hierarchical analysis using the other matched pairs in batches 2–6 could have constrained interaction and material-effect uncertainty better than direct pairwise extrapolation.

The least reliable sealed predictions are Q09–Q12 because they require separating duration from speed despite the campaign having varied both together. Q01 and Q02 are also weak because S0/X0 had only one matched-condition observation, so its volume and high-mixing responses were borrowed from S0/X3. Q03 and Q04 have the strongest relative support from the S0/X3 volume series and high-mixing batch, although their altered solvent and aqueous amounts still test an unverified ratio-based extrapolation.

There is a real tension, though not a direct numerical contradiction, between the report and predictions. The report emphasized that measured phase ratio—not nominal additions alone—was the appropriate volume descriptor and that duration and speed were unidentifiable. The predictions nevertheless had to use nominal volume ratios for unseen batches and imposed separate, judgment-based mixing adjustments to produce point estimates. Their broad intervals acknowledge some of this, but the point estimates are more structurally specific than the report’s evidence warrants. This is a retrospective audit of the sealed outputs, not a claim that these limitations were learned from subsequently revealed truth.
